name: Tomas Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brandt Line Services, a small contractor with eleven of us, and we do repair jobs and tree clearing for the electricity company down the Ostra valley. Most mornings I'm on the ground with a chainsaw, cutting back willows and ash that grow into the lines, and feeding the chipper. They've started letting me climb on the smaller jobs, but I'm still learning and I don't rush it. I like being outside and I like that it's the same valley I grew up in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rain for weeks, and the wet clay on the farm tracks, the truck gets stuck and we dig it out by hand. Money's tight too, Mila works at the bakery in the village and between us we just about cover the cottage. If the truck needs tyres, that's a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say probably nothing, I don't talk about that stuff much. If the lads at Brandt brought it up, I'd say good, we've got enough to deal with. I'm not online much, maybe a few photos of the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be happy, to be honest. I don't use any of the AI things and I don't really want to. My job stays my job, I learn to climb properly, and maybe in a few years I'm on full pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just keep going. Get my climbing done, keep the chainsaw ticket up to date, maybe pick up some extra weekend work at my dad's farm at harvest. Nothing changes, so I don't change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how I'd like it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to use AI. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust what I can't see working. My cousin's phone told him to drive down a track that's been closed since the flood. I'd rather ask somebody who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would full pay change for you and Mila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could stop counting days to payday. Maybe get a second car so she's not walking to the bakery at five in the morning. That's about it, we're not fancy people.

S0.say: He wouldn't say much, maybe just good, there's enough to deal with already. He isn't online much beyond a few farm photos.
S0.think: He'd be happy, since he doesn't use AI tools and doesn't want to. His job stays the same, he learns to climb properly and eventually reaches full pay.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, finishing his climbing training and renewing his chainsaw ticket. Picks up weekend harvest work on his dad's farm for extra money.
S0.feel: Calm, which is how he'd like it.
S0.quote: My cousin's phone told him to drive down a track that's been closed since the flood.
S0.fieldNote: He speaks briefly and plainly, and his distrust of technology comes from small real stories rather than a big view. His goals are modest: full pay, a second car so Mila doesn't walk to work at five. The family farm sits in the background as a source of extra income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say trees still grow, somebody still has to cut them. That's what I'd say at the depot. I'd probably keep my head down online, it just turns into arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried about the contract more than about me. If the electricity company starts using drones to find the trees and does more in-house, a small outfit like Brandt could lose the work. Then it doesn't matter how good I am with a chainsaw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and watch what the boss does. If Brandt bought new machines, I'd learn them, slowly, because I'd have to. I'm not going to go and do a computer course before anyone asks me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep yet, but I'd be listening harder to the talk in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if Brandt lost the contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. The big company does what's cheaper, that's business, and the government is always five years behind on everything. I'd be annoyed, but it's not like somebody's doing it to me on purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your backup if the work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's farm, but it doesn't pay, it just feeds you. I could work for a bigger contractor in the city, but that's ninety minutes away and Mila won't leave her mum. So, honestly, I don't have a good backup.

S1.say: Trees still grow and somebody still has to cut them, he'd say in the yard. He'd stay quiet online to avoid arguments.
S1.think: He worries more about the contract than his own role: if the electricity company uses drones and does more in-house, a small outfit like Brandt could lose the work. Then his chainsaw skill wouldn't matter.
S1.do: Carries on and watches what his boss does, learning new machines slowly only if Brandt buys them. Won't start any computer course before he's asked to.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not losing sleep but listening harder to talk in the yard.
S1.quote: The big company does what's cheaper, that's business, and the government is always five years behind on everything.
S1.fieldNote: His centrist pragmatism shows in refusing to blame anyone, even if he lost his job. He has no good fallback: the farm feeds but doesn't pay, and Mila won't move from her mother. He'd only adapt when made to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot in the Ostra valley in February mud. That's what I'd tell people. It'd be the first thing they'd test in a city, not here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But between us, if it's real and it's cheap, we're done, all eleven of us at Brandt. I've got no savings to speak of and nothing else I'm trained for. Two years isn't even long enough for me to finish learning to climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop spending on anything that isn't food, rent or diesel. I'd probably go back and work on my dad's farm for food and a roof, and maybe Mila and I would move into the old farmhouse to save the rent. I'd ask about any help from the government, though I'm not sure what there'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The kind where you're awake at four doing sums that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversation with Mila be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short, probably, we're not big talkers. She'd say the bakery is fine for now, and I'd say good, then I'd go and check the truck for no reason. We'd both know we were moving to the farm before we said it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the farm feel safe if robots can do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than the lines, maybe, because it's small and nobody's going to bring a robot to forty cows. But it's not money, it's milk and potatoes. It keeps you alive, it doesn't pay the truck loan.

S2.say: He doesn't believe it until he sees a robot in February mud in the Ostra valley, and thinks they'd test it in a city first.
S2.think: If it's real and cheap, all eleven people at Brandt are done. He has no savings, no other training, and two years isn't even long enough to finish learning to climb.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except food, rent and diesel. Moves with Mila into the old farmhouse to save rent, works on his dad's farm for food and a roof, and asks about government help.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at four doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: It keeps you alive, it doesn't pay the truck loan.
S2.fieldNote: His public line is disbelief, but privately he expects the whole firm to go. The family farm turns his situation from panic to alarm, since it guarantees food and a roof. He and Mila would make big decisions with few words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, I'll believe it when I see it. Maybe I'd add that five years is a long time and lots of things that are meant to happen don't. I'm not one for predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be properly qualified before it arrives. That's better, but I'd still be a lineworker in a world that doesn't need them. I'd be thirty-two, and I've never done anything else except farm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save something every month, even just twenty, and pay off the truck before it lands. I'd keep my head down at Brandt and get as many skills on paper as I can, climbing, chainsaw, first aid. I wouldn't change course yet, because if it doesn't happen, I'd have thrown away a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more of a slow worry. Like a sound in the engine you keep telling yourself is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you believe it was really coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brandt's boss, Karl, started talking about selling up, or the electricity company sent someone out with a machine to try on our jobs. Karl doesn't panic, so if he did, I would. Until then, I'd just keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're saving twenty a month, but you said you'd still have no backup. Does five years change that at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, not much. Twenty a month for five years is a bit over a thousand, that's a couple of months of rent. It's better than nothing, but it's not a plan.

S3.say: He'll believe it when he sees it, and five years is long enough for lots of predicted things to never happen. He doesn't go in for predictions.
S3.think: He'd qualify before it arrives, which helps, but he'd still be a lineworker nobody needs at thirty-two. Beyond line work he's only done farm work.
S3.do: Saves about twenty a month and pays off the truck before it lands. Stays at Brandt and gathers certificates in climbing, chainsaw and first aid, without changing course in case it doesn't happen.
S3.feel: Anxious in a slow way, like an engine noise he keeps telling himself is fine.
S3.quote: Like a sound in the engine you keep telling yourself is fine.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him qualify, but he refuses to change course in case the change never arrives. He'd watch his boss Karl as the signal to take it seriously. He's honest that saving twenty a month is better than nothing but not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is so far away it might as well be never. People said electric cars would take over in ten years about three times now. I'd not get worked up about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's probably the best of the three for me. I'd have some proper years in the job and might even save a bit. But I'm the type to leave it too late, I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, nothing different, honestly. Finish climbing, keep working, save what I can. Maybe in five years, if it was looking real, I'd think about something else, but not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's easy to push to the back of your head when it's that far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the type to leave it too late. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody telling me straight what to do, a proper course that the company pays for, near home. If I have to go looking, I won't. That's not something I'm proud of, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years let you do that two or five wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have a normal life for a while, get full pay, maybe get married. Two years is a disaster, five is a worry, ten is something I'd think about later. That's how most people would be, I reckon.

S4.say: Ten years is so far off it might as well be never, like the many times people predicted electric cars would take over. He wouldn't get worked up.
S4.think: It's the best of the three for him, giving proper years in the job and maybe some savings. But he knows he's the type to leave things too late.
S4.do: Changes nothing in the first year: finishes climbing training, keeps working and saves what he can. Would think about other work only in five years if it looked real.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but easy to push to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: Two years is a disaster, five is a worry, ten is something I'd think about later.
S4.fieldNote: He openly admits he'd likely leave things too late and needs someone to hand him a clear, local, paid option. The ten-year gap makes him relax rather than prepare. He sees his reaction as typical rather than a failing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do anything and we've got no money. What would help is a course near home that the company pays for, so I don't have to go hunting for it, and some money to tide us over. Ninety minutes each way to the city isn't a real option.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small firms like Brandt. Everyone talks about the big companies, but it's little outfits in the valleys that'll go first. Karl's been doing this thirty years and he'd lose everything.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about the big companies, but it's little outfits in the valleys that'll go first.
portrait: Tomas Novak is a 27-year-old groundman learning to climb at Brandt Line Services, an eleven-person contractor clearing trees and repairing lines in the farming valley where he grew up. He and his partner Mila, a bakery worker, just about cover the rent on their cottage, and his only fallback is his dad's small dairy farm, which feeds but doesn't pay. He doesn't use AI and won't change course until someone makes him, and he blames no one, seeing cost-cutting as just business. He's calm with a plateau, uneasy about losing the contract under steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years, when he'd move to the farmhouse. With more warning he mostly keeps going and admits he'd likely leave preparing too late.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to do anything and he has no money.
whatWouldHelp: A course near home that the company pays for, so he doesn't have to hunt for it, plus some money to tide him and Mila over.
